A.explanation: This is $200 \times 20 \times \sin 40^{\circ} \approx 2.6 \text{ kJ}$, the work of the vertical component which does not act along the horizontal displacement.

B.explanation: This is $200 \times 20 \times \cos 40^{\circ} \approx 3.1 \text{ kJ}$, the horizontal component of tension times horizontal displacement.

C.explanation: This value is larger than $F d \cos 40^{\circ}$ and does not follow from the $200 \text{ N}$, $20 \text{ m}$ and $40^{\circ}$ projection.

D.explanation: This is $200 \times 20 = 4.0 \text{ kJ}$, which ignores the $40^{\circ}$ angle and treats the full tension as acting along the path.

hints: Notice the $200 \text{ N}$ tension acts at $40^{\circ}$ to the $20 \text{ m}$ horizontal displacement, so only part of the force pulls along the path.
Recall work by an angled constant force is $W = F d \cos \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between force and displacement.
Calculate the horizontal component $200 \cos 40^{\circ}$ in $\text{N}$, then multiply by $20 \text{ m}$ and convert the result in $\text{J}$ to $\text{kJ}$.
walkthrough: Identify the given data: force $F = 200 \text{ N}$, displacement $d = 20 \text{ m}$ horizontally, and angle between them $\theta = 40^{\circ}$.
State the rule: only the component of force in the direction of motion does work, so $W = F d \cos \theta$.
Find the effective pulling force: $F_{x} = F \cos 40^{\circ} = 200 \times \cos 40^{\circ} \approx 200 \times 0.766 \approx 153 \text{ N}$.
Check units and size: $1 \text{ J} = 1 \text{ N m}$, so $3060 \text{ J} \approx 3.1 \text{ kJ}$, which matches the $\text{kJ}$ options and is less than $Fd = 4.0 \text{ kJ}$. This is option B.
